title: ‘Fur Lives Matter’ case turns heads as DOJ’s ‘Fraud Week’ targets taxpayer swindlers
summary: A Missouri man allegedly stole a real company's identity to seek $56 million in PPP and SBA funds during Colin McDonald's "Fraud Week" crackdown.
story: Western Missouri U.S. Attorney Matt Price explains how the eye-catching case fits into a broader federal push targeting more than $245 million in intended losses tied to SBA fraud.

A nationwide business-aid fraud crackdown — highlighted by a bizarre Missouri scheme involving alleged stolen corporate identity — is among the enforcement actions being highlighted during the federal push dubbed "Fraud Week."

The announcement is part of the Department of Justice's National Fraud Enforcement Division's nationwide summer surge. It netted more than 160 criminal defendants and approximately $245 million in intended losses to taxpayers, according to DOJ, as the agency announced busts from Los Angeles to Philadelphia.

"This is the problem of our day," said U.S. Attorney Matt Price of the Western District of Missouri, whose office was one of 44 involved in the greater "Heartland Fraud Surge" that encompassed June through Sept. 1. "And this is a response to what happened over the previous four years,"
WHITE HOUSE PUSHES 'WATERSHED' FRAUD-FIGHTING REFORM IN CONGRESS AS VANCE CONVENES TASK FORCE

Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks during a news conference announcing what federal officials described as the largest healthcare fraud takedown in U.S. history, resulting in charges against 455 defendants nationwide. (Ken Cedeno/AFP via Getty Image)

"After 9/11, there was a huge lean-in, [an] all-of-government approach to national security issues," Price said, comparing the Bush-era interagency pivot to terror threats with the coordinated response to the current push against fraud in taxpayer-funded programs.
Price headlined the extensive Small Business Administration (SBA) and COVID-19-related fraud probes under division chief Colin McDonald.

In the "Fur Lives Matter" case, a Missouri man allegedly claimed to operate 19 separate businesses, including some focused on pet care like "Fur Lives Matter," "Fur Lives Matter LLC," "Chows & Pals" and "God’s Chow Chow."
MINNESOTA FRAUD MASTERMIND GETS NEARLY 42 YEARS IN PRISON IN MASSIVE $250M 'FEEDING OUR FUTURE' SCHEME

The Small Business Administration suspended more than 100,000 California borrowers amid nearly $9 billion in suspected pandemic-era loan fraud, SBA Administrator Kelly Loeffler announced Friday. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
There was one glaring problem: "Fur Lives Matter" was a real company in another state — and prosecutors say it had no connection to Gray.

Using "Fur Lives Matter" and the other purported companies, Jamie Gray allegedly sought to fraudulently obtain nearly $56 million in Paycheck Protection (PPP) and Economic Injury Disaster (EIDL) funds from the Small Business Administration through 29 applications.
BRAZEN SOCIAL MEDIA FRAUD SCHEMES WREAK HAVOC AS TRUMP OFFICIAL ISSUES STARK WARNING FOR 'FRAUDFLUENCERS'
Most cases involved entirely fictitious businesses, and only "Fur Lives Matter" was operational at the Feb. 15, 2020, eligibility cutoff.

"Gray effectively stole this company’s identity," the DOJ said in a statement, alleging the legitimate business had no knowledge of him and that his claims about ownership, employees, revenue and operations were fabricated. Gray nevertheless received about $820,000 in SBA funds, prosecutors said.
The case stood out even among a summer surge of alleged fraud schemes for its unusual details.
JUDGE SENTENCES FEEDING OUR FUTURE FRAUDSTERS WHO FAKED RUNNING CHILD NUTRITION SITE

"If you screwed the American taxpayer, the federal government is now going to say you're cut off, no more," Vice President JD Vance said this week on the matter of the larger administration crackdown. "You shouldn't be applying anymore, and if you do apply, you're no longer able to get those benefits."
VANCE-LED TASK FORCE CUTS OFF $1.4B FROM HOME HEALTH, HOSPICE PROVIDERS SUSPECTED OF FRAUD
Price said the effort is expanding beyond Operation No Doze, the SBA-focused enforcement action conducted as part of the broader Heartland Fraud Surge.
His office and Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe, along with other state officials, have also launched Operation Show-Me the Money, a new state-federal effort targeting fraud in state benefit programs.
REPUBLICANS DECLARE WAR ON 'ORGANIZED THEFT' WITH GOVERNMENT FRAUD CRACKDOWN

"No fraud is too small to prosecute, but leveraging all state resources in the state of Missouri from the top down [is believed to be] a first-of-its-kind collaboration between the state and the feds, working to identify and prosecute this type of fraud," he said Saturday.
Price also credited SBA Administrator Kelly Loeffler with "leading from the front" as the agency is suspending suspected fraudulent borrowers and sending demand letters seeking repayment.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
He said the Heartland Surge depicts a new approach to countering fraud, characterizing the Biden administration’s attempts to recoup lost dollars as a "pay and chase" model.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Attorney General Todd Blanche has instructed prosecutors to charge fraud cases of all sizes, in that the smaller cases send the message to bigger scofflaws that, no matter the amount of money involved, "if you ripped off the American taxpayer… we will find you, we will identify you, we will hunt you down, we'll prosecute you," said Price.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: A look inside program giving future Nat Sec experts 5-year head start amid evolving threats: ‘Ready day one’
summary: Seton Hall University's national security fellowship pairs graduate students with government agencies to research China, AI and foreign influence.
story: Fox News Digital spoke to Seton Hall national security fellow Mohamad Mirghahari about the changing landscape of national security and his program equipping students for placement in high levels of government.

As the United States confronts increasingly complex threats from China, foreign influence, artificial intelligence and geopolitical flashpoints around the world, one Seton Hall University program is giving graduate students hands-on experience tackling real national security challenges before they enter the workforce at a rate its founder says proves the program’s importance.

The National Security Graduate Fellowship at Seton Hall’s School of Diplomacy and International Relations pairs students with government agencies seeking research and analysis on pressing foreign policy and national security issues and has an 80% placement rate, with graduates going on to work at the NSA, CIA, Secret Service, military and defense contracting companies, according to founder Mohamad Mirghahari.
"My goal for my students is they’re ready day one if they get hired," Mirghahari told Fox News Digital.

Mirghahari, a Seton Hall graduate and national security expert who spent 14 years in key Department of Defense leadership roles supporting counterterrorism initiatives around the globe, later served as a presidential appointee and senior advisor to the Transportation Security Administration’s chief of staff and remains a special advisor to the Defense Department.
US COUNTERINTELLIGENCE ‘WAY BEHIND,’ POST-9/11 RECORD ‘EXTRAORDINARILY NEGLIGENT’, FMR TRUMP WH OFFICIAL WARNS

Fox News Digital spoke to Seton Hall national security fellow Mohamad Mirghahari about the changing landscape of national security and his program equipping students for placement in high levels of government. (Fox Digital iStock)

"Our program is unlike any other in the nation because our graduate students are actually tackling real-world national security challenges and issues from government agencies," Mirghahari explained. "As we know, most government agencies have a lot of things going on and they don't have enough resources, but what our graduate students are able to do is support those government agencies, answering and doing research for real-world requirements in the national security field."

Mirghahari says the program is also unique due to the practitioners from "across the United States government" that serve as guest lecturers and professors giving students a necessary insight into experiences in the field, particularly given the changing landscape and variety of threats facing the nation compared to 10 or 20 years ago.
INTEL CHIEF WARNS OF 'EVOLVING' THREATS AS TERROR GROUPS NOW 'RECRUIT THEIR AGENTS ONLINE'
Aerial view of the Pentagon building in Arlington, Va., on Oct. 22, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images))

"Part of what makes our program so unique is that we address the real-world issues of today," Mirghahari said. "History is very important, and you learn from history, but we also want to be the classes that can support the government in real time. We have done projects on China, India and Pakistan, as well as the South China Sea."

The fellowship’s work has included projects for the State Department on how the U.S. could re-engage with the Taliban if the group returned to power in Afghanistan. Mirghahari said the research remained relevant for years, with the papers later recirculated within the government.
"That’s part of what we do, provide that real-time research," he said.

The program also focuses on emerging national security challenges involving artificial intelligence, data and foreign influence. Mirghahari said younger students often bring valuable technological expertise and perspectives that government agencies may not have previously considered.
"Artificial intelligence, data and all these different things impacting our national security play a major role in our work," he said.

On the artificial intelligence front, which has changed how the United States deals with cyber threats along with how it conducts cyber operations, Mirghahari says it has become a "force multiplier" for his students.

"We examine foreign influence, including how data is mined and distributed, and we use tools such as artificial intelligence, graph theory and other analytical methods to examine large datasets," he said. "We’re giving students an awareness of these technologies and how they can be used across the government.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
College students raise their hands to answer a question during class. (Getty Images)

Mirghahari added, "Our students can sift through large amounts of information and extract what is relevant to support their research. That process is extremely time-consuming, so we’re helping government clients bring the information together in one place and examine it more thoroughly."

Mirghahari told Fox News Digital he believes students would need to work for five years in a national security position to be able to learn the on the job skills they learn at the Seton Hall program and explained that now, perhaps more than ever, hitting the ground running is critically important.
"Some of the feedback we’ve received from agencies is, ‘Your students are well-equipped. They’re better than some of the people who have been here for five to 10 years,’" Mirghahari said.
Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter at Fox News. Find him on Twitter @andymarkmiller and email tips to AndrewMark.Miller@Fox.com.

title: WATCH: Americans warn AI will take jobs despite reassuring labor data: ‘Just wait’
summary: Americans sound the alarm over AI taking jobs, but a Yale Budget Lab report found no link between AI adoption and changes in employment rates.
story: Fox News Digital spoke with people critical of what's in store for the future following a new report by the Bureau of Economic Analysis showing that artificial intelligence has boosted the economy, rather than causing the employment rate to tank.

As debate intensifies over the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), people are sounding the alarm about the technology's potential to disrupt the American workforce and displace workers.
"Maybe not yet, but it is certainly going to happen imminently," Max from South Africa said about the risk of AI taking jobs away from Americans.
"The amount of AI that's pushing and talkbots that you can use and systems that will allow you to sidestep other individuals or systems, it's on its way," Max said.
DEMOCRATS SOUND ALARM OVER AI JOB APOCALYPSE — BUT LABOR MARKET ISN'T FOLLOWING SCRIPT

People are weighing the threat artificial intelligence poses to workers to Fox News Digital as AI infrastructure rapidly expands and new research finds little evidence of significant job losses so far. (Nicholas Ballasy/Fox News Digital; Mikala Compton/The Austin American-Statesman/Getty Images)
"Everybody's probably going to get fired, just wait," Ivory from Virginia told Fox News Digital.
The reactions come after a shocking new report by the Budget Lab at Yale revealed that recent research shows no connection between the rapid adoption of AI and changes in employment rates.

"I think maybe folks are afraid… that there will not be any humans needed to run things, but I think that's not the case," Crystal from Pennsylvania said. "You're going to need the people to still implement the AI."
A recent paper by the Bureau of Economic Analysis similarly found that AI use has not been linked to any significant decline in employment, and is instead associated with stronger economic growth.
Others that Fox News Digital spoke with dismissed the report’s results, suggesting AI adoption will inevitably spike job layoffs.
"I don’t believe it," Henry from Virginia said when asked about the recent report.
He continued, "You take any business…. They're all training to make people available and able to work with AI. And the net of it is that the nose count goes down."
SEN. BERNIE SANDERS: YES, WE MUST HIT THE PAUSE BUTTON ON AI BEFORE IT IS TOO LATE
Another person Fox News Digital spoke with disagreed, arguing AI is "not there yet" in its ability to replace human intelligence.
"We thought that it could replace software developers and coders right off the bat," he said. "Fortunately for us, but unfortunately for AI, we're not there yet. "

AI has been at the forefront of conversation in Washington, with President Donald Trump urging against tech experts’ call for a slowdown in the development of AI to allow humans to keep up with its rapidly accelerating pace. Prominent Democrats, including former President Barack Obama, are pleading for the slowdown despite previously promoting its economic potential.

"We have an energy crisis," a person who spoke with Fox News Digital said. "We don't have enough energy to really take AI to the next level. At this point, I think moving forward next decade, we'll see a lot of changes. But as of right now, when you lay off the panic button, I think we're just fine."
ONE MONTHLY BILL AMERICANS CAN’T AVOID IS QUIETLY SURGING THANKS TO EMERGING INDUSTRY: DATA

Virginia has long been at the center of America’s data center industry, with Northern Virginia now the largest data center market in the world and home to roughly 13% of global operational capacity. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

While America is producing record amounts of crude oil, the expansion of data centers is projected to ramp up electricity demand in the U.S. to record levels in the coming years, according to the Energy Information Administration. It is estimated that a large data center will require as much electricity as a small city, Fed researchers found.

The looming uncertainty over the impact of AI in the future is prompting workers to consider how to prepare for an AI-powered economy, despite the data not yet confirming the fears of impacting employment rates.
"You need to know how it works and get good at using it," Harvey from London said.
"I think it's just going to propel us forward and we have to keep up," Crystal said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
She continued, "If we don't, what’s next?"
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: Justice Department charges 16 across multiple states with alleged illegal voting, election crimes
summary: The Department of Justice charged 16 people across multiple states for alleged illegal voting, with eight noncitizens in Texas among those accused.
story: DHS Sec. Markwayne Mullin joins 'Saturday in America' to highlight border enforcement updates and criticize the Biden administration border policies following 16 straight months of zero releases under current enforcement. He reiterates that DHS and ICE remain committed to targeting high-risk individuals to keep American communities safe.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) announced charges against 16 people in multiple states in connection with alleged illegal voting, voter registration and other election-related crimes, including cases involving noncitizens accused of casting ballots in federal elections.

DOJ followed the announcement with a warning on social media, saying some of those charged allegedly voted in the 2022 and 2024 elections, and warning others against attempting to illegally participate in U.S. elections.
"Let this be a warning to ANYONE trying to cheat and undermine our elections," the DOJ wrote. "Spread the word!"
According to DOJ, eight noncitizens residing in Texas were charged, while the other cases involved defendants in Idaho, Georgia, Massachusetts, Wisconsin, New Jersey and Michigan.
SKID ROW FORGERIES, ILLEGAL VOTES AND A MAYORAL CANDIDATE: ELECTION FRAUD CASES PILE UP NATIONWIDE

The Justice Department announced charges against 16 people across multiple states in connection with alleged illegal voting, voter registration and other election-related crimes. (The Justice Department)
The allegations include noncitizens voting in federal elections, false claims of U.S. citizenship to register or vote and false statements related to naturalization.
During the investigations, the DOJ said authorities also uncovered alleged passport and identification fraud, wire fraud and firearm-related offenses.
The cases are part of a broader Trump administration enforcement effort targeting alleged illegal voting and election-related crimes.
WATCH: ILLEGAL ALIEN BUSTED IN BATTLEGROUND STATE AFTER ALLEGEDLY COMMITTING VOTER FRAUD

Mexican national Monica Carzoli, 46, a lawful permanent resident, admitted to registering to vote and voting in the November 2024 election, according to the Justice Department. She was arrested this week in Del Rio, Texas. (Department of Justice)

In Georgia, DOJ said Analiea Milliscent Eccles, a Venezuelan national and DACA recipient, voted nine times between 2008 and 2024. She was charged with voting as a noncitizen and falsely claiming U.S. citizenship to vote.

Avila Gomez, a Mexican national residing in Idaho, is accused of falsely claiming U.S. citizenship to register to vote and then voting in May 2022 and November 2024. The indictment also includes wire fraud, passport, identification-document and firearm-related charges.

DOJ said Santana Coulibaly, a lawful permanent resident in New Jersey, registered to vote in 2016, voted in federal elections in 2018 and 2020 and submitted a provisional ballot in the 2024 presidential election. She also faces allegations involving statements made in her naturalization applications.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the DOJ's Fraud Division told Fox News that the Trump administration has now charged 50 noncitizens with illegal voting.
ICE ARRESTS PERUVIAN NATIONAL ACCUSED OF ILLEGALLY VOTING IN 2024 ELECTION AS DHS CITES SIMILAR CASES

Nigerian national Gladys Adaeze Okafor, 56, a lawful permanent resident, was arrested and charged with illegally voting in the 2022 elections and allegedly voting in the 2024 general election, according to the Justice Department. (The Department of Justice)
"America's elections are for Americans," McDonald said.
In a separate interview, Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin said a broader investigation was underway.
Mullin said officials have more than 1,620 open cases and have made 151 arrests. He also said authorities are looking into more than 300,000 suspected cases, a figure he said continues to grow.
ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ARRESTED IN INDIANA FOR ALLEGEDLY VOTING IN FEDERAL ELECTION: DHS

Colombian national Julieta Englestad, 53, a lawful permanent resident, is facing charges for allegedly falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen when registering to vote in the November 2022 federal election, according to the Justice Department. (The Department of Justice)
Mullin asserted that "every single vote that was at the hands of an illegal [immigrant], canceled out a citizen that was legally registered and able to vote."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"One is too many, but the fact that we have 300,000 cases we're looking into right now and 1,620 cases that are under investigation, and 151 arrests is unacceptable," Mullin said.
The Justice Department noted that the charges announced Friday are accusations and that all defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.
Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: NORAD F-16 intercepts aircraft that violated restricted airspace over Camp David with Trump present: officials
summary: A NORAD F-16 reportedly intercepted an aircraft violating restricted airspace over Camp David Saturday while President Donald Trump stayed there.
story: An F-16 fighter jet was caught on camera closing in on a small airplane near Jefferson Township, New Jersey, outside Trump's Bedminster golf club, where temporary flight restrictions were in place. (Credit: X / Joe Afflerbach)
A NORAD F-16 fighter jet intercepted an aircraft that violated restricted airspace over the area of Camp David Saturday morning while President Donald Trump was there, according to officials.
There is a permanent no-fly zone over Camp David in Maryland, with additional restrictions when the president is there.

NORAD dispensed flares during the intercept to get the pilot’s attention and was able to safely escort the aircraft out of the area, the Defense Visual Information Distribution Service (DVIDS) said in a release.
NORAD F-16S INTERCEPT MULTIPLE AIRCRAFT VIOLATING TEMPORARY FLIGHT RESTRICTIONS OVER NEW JERSEY
A U.S. Air Force F-16 fighter in 2016 (SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Should NORAD aircraft intercept a general aviation aircraft, the pilot should immediately come up on frequency 121.5 or 243.0 and turn around to reverse course until receiving additional instructions on one of those frequencies," the release said.
NORAD F-16S INTERCEPT MULTIPLE AIRCRAFT VIOLATING FLIGHT RESTRICTIONS OVER NEW JERSEY
President Donald Trump leaving the White House on Marine One Friday evening. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)
Turmp left for Camp David Friday evening.

"Pilots! @NORADCommand fighter aircraft intercepted an aircraft violating restricted airspace over Thurmont, MD, resulting in flares being deployed," the First Air Force, part of NORAD, wrote on X Saturday.

A view of the main lodge at Camp David (Whitehouse.gov)

title: Trump announces new 'AI Force,' vows to protect industry as AI czar announcement nears
summary: Trump's new AI Force mirrors his first-term Space Force creation, with a high-IQ "czar" appointment coming soon to oversee the booming industry.
story: 'Outnumbered' panel analyzes requests from Anthropic and OpenAI executives for federal artificial intelligence regulation ahead of the midterm elections. They react to President Donald Trump's dismissal of doomsday scenarios and White House tech advisor David Sacks' opposition to development pauses.
President Donald Trump announced Saturday that he is creating an AI Force and plans to name an artificial intelligence czar as his administration pushes to accelerate the growth of AI in the U.S.

Trump said in a lengthy Truth Social post that his administration would resist efforts to restrict the rapidly developing technology while using the existing criminal and civil justice systems to address potential wrongdoing.
"We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," the post said. "Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!"
GOP LAWMAKERS SMELL SOMETHING ELSE BEHIND BIG TECH'S AI DOOMSDAY WARNINGS: 'SOMETHING ELSE GOING ON'
President Donald Trump displays a signed executive order related to his Artificial Intelligence Action Plan. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images, File)
Trump added that the government would also be "looking for BAD" and said existing criminal and civil laws could be used to address problems with the technology.

"For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term," the president's post continued. "To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI ‘Czar’ — Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!"
Trump did not provide details about the structure, authority or membership of the proposed AI Force or identify potential candidates to serve as its czar.
POWERFUL COLD WAR-ERA TOOL TRUMP COULD USE IN AN AI EMERGENCY IS SET TO EXPIRE IN DECEMBER
President Donald Trump displays a signed executive order during the Winning the AI Race summit in July 2025. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images, File)
Trump's announcement comes as lawmakers grapple with whether and how to regulate the rapidly developing technology.
Some Republicans have questioned calls for additional government oversight, while others have pushed for safeguards after AI industry leaders raised concerns about increasingly capable models.
Earlier this week, Trump joined the debate by rejecting calls for additional government regulation of the industry, arguing that restrictions could hinder the U.S. in its competition with China.
In Saturday’s post, Trump compared criticism of AI and data centers to several other political controversies and argued that opposition to data center construction had largely failed.
RAND PAUL CLASHES WITH FELLOW REPUBLICAN OVER AI 'KILL SWITCH' AS SENATE GRAPPLES WITH 'TERMINATOR' FEARS
The president's announcement Saturday comes as lawmakers grapple with whether and how to regulate the rapidly developing technology. (Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP via Getty Images, File)
Trump also predicted that AI could eventually account for as much as 25% of U.S. gross domestic product, though he did not cite a source for the estimate.

"AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country’s GDP," he wrote. "We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!"
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
In a separate Truth Social post, Trump asked people to choose within the post on what to call AI.

"Many people think that the words "Artificial Intelligence" are inaccurate, and very ineloquent, relative to AI, or Artificial Intelligence. A far more elegant and accurate description of this new phenomena would be Superior Intelligence (SI) or, Extreme Intelligence (EI) or, Supreme Intelligence (SI)," he wrote.
"This is a Poll, and I would appreciate everybody voting! Which is the best name for this ever growing "Revolution?" President DONALD J. TRUMP"
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Flying taxis are taking off in Texas. Is your city next?
summary: Joby Aviation flew its eVTOL air taxi into DFW Airport's busy airspace as Texas launches Project Nexus, a three-year advanced air mobility program.
story: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy addresses rising drone incidents near airports, detailing a recent JetBlue collision and discussing investigations. He unveils new FAA technology for civilian supersonic flights, aiming to reduce travel times. Duffy also highlights innovations in autonomous vehicles and drone deliveries, emphasizing balancing safety with advancing transportation technology across the country.

If you have ever watched your arrival time creep later while sitting in traffic, flying over it sounds pretty appealing. Texas is now testing what that could look like. Earlier this month, the Texas Department of Transportation launched the first phase of Project Nexus, a three-year program focused on preparing next-generation aircraft for use in Texas skies.

The Sept. 10 kickoff at Perot Field Fort Worth Alliance Airport included demonstrations from BETA Technologies and Joby Aviation. Joby brought its electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, better known as an eVTOL. No passengers climbed aboard the initial Project Nexus flights. Instead, Texas is starting to learn how air taxis could eventually fit into the way people get around.
NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, Sept. 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.
Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com.
AIR TAXIS CUT HOUR-LONG COMMUTES TO MINUTES, RIDERS MAY BE SHOCKED BY THE PRICE
Joby Aviation’s electric air taxi sits at Perot Field Fort Worth Alliance Airport, where the company has established its North Texas operating base. (Joby Aviation)
Flying taxi testing has officially started in Texas

Project Nexus will advance in phases over the next three years. The broader first phase uses traditional aircraft, including helicopters and fixed-wing planes, to test routes and collect data. TxDOT says those initial flights will help validate routes and prepare for future advanced air mobility operations. Joby also launched a week-long campaign of piloted electric air taxi flights across North Texas under TxDOT's Project Nexus proposal, part of the federal eVTOL Integration Pilot Program. The campaign included planned direct flights into DFW International Airport, a round trip to Arlington and a route connecting Alliance Airport with Toyota Motor North America's headquarters in Plano. One of the biggest tests involved DFW. Joby's campaign called for a direct flight into DFW's controlled airspace, with the aircraft landing at DFW Corporate Aviation. That puts an eVTOL into the same busy airspace used by one of the world's busiest airports. That kind of testing can tell regulators much more about how these aircraft might eventually operate around major transportation hubs.
Air taxis are getting closer to reality

We have been following electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, better known as eVTOLs, for years. They can rise vertically like a helicopter. Many designs then transition into forward flight using wings. Earlier this year, we looked at how a federal pilot program could bring air taxis into U.S. skies before the industry reaches full commercial service. We have also covered plans for air taxis serving New York City's three major airports and Joby's partnership with Virgin Atlantic to develop electric air taxi service in the United Kingdom. So the aircraft themselves are no longer the biggest surprise. What gets my attention now is where companies are flying them and how regulators are testing their ability to operate around airports people already use. That's where Project Nexus comes in.
Why Dallas-Fort Worth gives air taxis a serious test

Flying around Dallas-Fort Worth creates challenges you do not get at an isolated test site. Joby's campaign included planned missions between Perot Field Fort Worth Alliance Airport and several destinations around the region. DFW International Airport was part of that schedule. The company and federal researchers have been preparing for this type of operation for years. Joby says the FAA and NASA began studying electric air taxi integration in North Texas in 2018. Then, in 2023, Joby and NASA ran a detailed simulation examining whether the DFW terminal area could handle as many as 50 electric air taxi operations per hour. Now that work is moving from computer simulations to aircraft operating in North Texas. Joby has also leased a 45,000-square-foot facility at Perot Field Fort Worth Alliance Airport. The new facility gives Joby a long-term operating presence in North Texas, well beyond this initial flight campaign.
AI AIR TRAFFIC SYSTEM PROMISES FEWER FLIGHT DELAYS
Joby Aviation’s eVTOL takes to the skies as Texas tests how electric air taxis could operate in busy regional airspace. (Joby Aviation)
Project Nexus may move medical supplies before passengers

Here's where the Texas plan gets especially interesting. Air taxis tend to grab attention because people imagine hopping aboard and flying over traffic. But some early Project Nexus missions could have nothing to do with your commute. Later phases are expected to focus on medical and cargo logistics. TxDOT specifically points to transporting critical medical supplies or organs between rural facilities and urban medical centers in Austin and San Antonio. That's a use case that could be easier to understand than flying across town to save a few minutes. Moving time-sensitive medical supplies faster could show where this technology provides practical value while passenger operations continue developing.
Passenger air taxis come later

Eventually, Project Nexus plans to put passengers onboard. TxDOT says the final phase will involve passenger air taxi flights across the Texas Triangle. TxDOT's plan calls for regional air taxi connections involving Dallas, Austin, San Antonio and Houston. That does not mean commercial passenger service across Texas has a firm launch date. Joby still has certification work ahead. The company says it has advanced into the fifth and final stage of FAA type certification, with testing continuing as part of that process. So you probably will not see an air taxi button appear beside your rideshare options tomorrow. The work happening now is about figuring out how these aircraft could operate safely before passenger service expands.
Air taxi testing is spreading across the US

Texas is getting a lot of attention right now, but Project Nexus is part of a much larger federal effort. The eVTOL Integration Pilot Program includes eight projects across 26 states, with testing focused on passenger travel, cargo and medical transportation. We have already seen some of that play out. Earlier this month, we covered the FAA's testing of Elroy Air's pilotless hybrid-electric Chaparral cargo aircraft. BETA Technologies and United Therapeutics have also tested electric aircraft for transporting organs between Virginia and Maryland. Other projects involve New York and New Jersey, Florida and several additional states. So while Texas is one of the biggest air taxi test beds right now, it is far from the only one. That raises the bigger question: If these trials keep expanding, how long will it be before you start seeing aircraft like these closer to home?
DOORDASH GETS FAA APPROVAL FOR ITS OWN DELIVERY DRONES
Joby Aviation’s piloted electric air taxi flies over North Texas during Project Nexus testing. (Joby Aviation)
What this means to you

If air taxis eventually come to your area, the big question will be simple: Will they actually make your life easier? Skipping over traffic sounds great, especially on the way to an airport or across a crowded metro area. But the convenience depends on where these aircraft take off and land, how much a ride costs and how much time you really save from door to door. You will also want to know what frequent flights sound like overhead. Electric aircraft are designed to be quieter than helicopters, but there is a big difference between hearing one occasionally and having them fly regularly near your neighborhood. And before any of this becomes routine, the FAA has to be comfortable with the safety side. That's exactly why these Texas tests are important. They give regulators a chance to see how the aircraft handle busy airspace before passenger flights become more common. For me, that is what makes Project Nexus worth watching. We already know these aircraft can fly. Now we are starting to find out whether they can fit into the way we actually travel.
Kurt's key takeaways

I have been watching air taxis develop for years, but Project Nexus feels like the kind of test that can tell us whether they have a real shot at becoming useful transportation. Flying around North Texas and operating at DFW gives Joby a chance to show how these aircraft can handle the kind of busy airspace they would face in regular service. I am also really interested in the medical side. If an electric aircraft can move an organ or critical supplies faster between hospitals, that could be one of the first places where this technology shows its value. For passengers, though, I still come back to two things: price and convenience. If the landing site is 30 minutes out of your way or the fare costs a fortune, flying over traffic starts to lose some of its appeal. Noise will also be something communities pay close attention to as more of these aircraft take to the sky. We already know air taxis can fly. What I want to see now is whether they can save you enough time, at a price you can live with, to make you actually want to book one.
If an air taxi could turn an hour in traffic into a 15-minute flight, how much would you be willing to pay to take it? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Scammers are buying Google ads to steal bank logins
summary: Federal prosecutors say criminals bought sponsored search ads mimicking real banks, capturing over 5,000 login credentials and draining accounts.
story: Cybercrime losses reached nearly $21 billion last year, prompting Kurt Knutsson to warn of increasingly sophisticated AI scams. He joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to break down the FBI data, highlighting that investment fraud alone cost victims $8.65 billion. Knutsson hosts a free live class to teach families how to protect their money and secure accounts.
You need to check your bank account, so you open Google, type in your bank's name and click the first result that looks right. Most of us have done some version of that without thinking twice.

Now federal investigators say criminals turned that everyday habit into a way to steal bank logins and drain accounts. The Justice Department announced on Sept. 8 that a Russian web developer accused of helping run a large bank account takeover operation had been extradited to the United States. Prosecutors say the group bought sponsored search engine links that sent banking customers to fake login pages. Victims then entered their credentials, believing they had reached their bank.

That should get the attention of anyone who banks online. Here's how the scam works, why those sponsored results can look so convincing and what you can do to avoid handing your bank login to a criminal.
ASKED SIRI TO CALL YOUR BANK? A SCAM COULD COST THOUSANDS

Federal investigators say the alleged scheme captured more than 5,000 stolen login credentials and caused millions of dollars in losses. (Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
How the fake bank ad scam worked

According to federal prosecutors, the alleged operation used spoofed domains that mimicked websites belonging to federally insured financial institutions. The conspirators then bought sponsored search engine links. Those links could appear when someone searched for their bank.

A click sent the customer to a fraudulent login page. Once victims entered their credentials, the attackers could capture that information. Prosecutors say the group then used the stolen credentials to access real bank accounts, check balances and initiate unauthorized wire transfers.

The indictment also alleges that Sergei Anatolyevich Filimonov developed and maintained infrastructure supporting the operation. That included databases storing more than 5,000 stolen login credentials and software designed to capture sensitive authentication data.
Where Google and Bing come into the story

The newest Sept. 8 Justice Department announcement says the conspirators purchased sponsored search-engine links. It does not name a particular search engine. However, the DOJ previously described the same bank account takeover operation when it seized the group's backend domain in December 2025. In that announcement, investigators specifically said the criminal group delivered fraudulent advertisements through search engines including Google and Bing. The ads imitated sponsored search ads used by legitimate banks.

Victims who clicked those ads were redirected to fake banking websites controlled by the criminals, according to the DOJ. That earlier investigation had identified at least 19 victims across the United States by December 2025. The DOJ reported approximately $28 million in attempted losses and about $14.6 million in actual losses tied to those victims.

Microsoft told CyberGuy that it has policies and detection mechanisms designed to help prevent misleading advertising. The company said that when it becomes aware of ads that violate its policies, it takes action to remove them and uses what it learns to strengthen its detection capabilities. Microsoft also encourages users to report suspicious ads through its "Report a Concern" form. We also reached out to Google for comment but did not hear back before our deadline.
FAKE PATIENT PORTAL SCAM CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN AND INFECT YOUR PC
Using your bank’s official app or a trusted bookmark can help you avoid fraudulent search results designed to steal your account information. (Neil Godwin/Future via Getty Images)
Why a sponsored Google result can fool you

The trap works because a paid search result can appear in a place many of us naturally look first. You search for your bank. A result appears near the top. The wording looks familiar, so you click before studying the address. Most search ads are legitimate.

Still, the FBI warns that criminals can buy ads that imitate real businesses and direct users to convincing phishing sites. The FBI refers to this tactic as SEO poisoning in its account takeover guidance. That changes how I would approach something as sensitive as online banking. In fact, the FBI specifically recommends using bookmarks or favorites to reach login pages rather than clicking search results or advertisements.
Bank account takeover losses have topped $262 million

This problem stretches far beyond one alleged criminal operation. Since January 2025, the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center has received more than 5,100 complaints reporting account takeover fraud. Reported losses have exceeded $262 million.

Criminals use several ways to get inside accounts. Fraudulent banking websites remain one of them. The FBI says victims can encounter a phishing site after clicking a fake search advertisement. Attackers may also try to obtain a one-time passcode if an account uses multifactor authentication.
Once criminals gain access, they may move money to accounts they control. That can make recovery difficult, especially when funds move quickly.
The accused developer has now been extradited to the U.S.

The latest development centers on Sergei Anatolyevich Filimonov, 36, a Russian national and web developer. A federal grand jury indicted Filimonov on Nov. 4, 2025. Authorities later extradited him from the Republic of Georgia.
Tips to protect yourself from fake bank login ads
You do not need to stop banking online. However, changing how you reach your bank's login page can lower your risk.
SHOULD YOU USE A SEPARATE COMPUTER FOR ONLINE BANKING?

If you already have your bank's verified app installed, open it directly rather than searching for your bank in a browser. That removes the search-result step where this particular scam tries to catch you.

Visit your bank's verified website and save it as a bookmark or favorite. The FBI specifically recommends bookmarks or favorites for financial login pages instead of relying on search results or advertisements.

Take a second to inspect the domain before you enter banking credentials. A fake site may use a misspelled address or another small change designed to look legitimate. The FBI warns that fraudulent search ads can lead to URLs that closely resemble the real address. Microsoft also advises users to carefully review website URLs before entering credentials or other personal information online.
A routine Google search can lead to a convincing fake bank login page when criminals buy sponsored ads that mimic trusted financial institutions. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
A "Sponsored" label means someone paid to place the advertisement. So when money or sensitive information is involved, verify the destination yourself before you sign in.

Enable two-factor or multifactor authentication if your financial institution offers it. However, do not let that give you a false sense of security. The FBI warns that MFA may not protect you after you land on a fraudulent login page. Criminals can also use social engineering to try to obtain your one-time code. Never give a one-time passcode to someone who contacts you unexpectedly.
YOUR BANK MAY STOP TEXTING YOU SIX-DIGIT CODES

A trusted password manager can help because it associates your saved login with a particular website. If your password manager normally fills your banking credentials but suddenly does not, stop before typing them manually. Check the address first. We've previously explained how password managers can provide another clue when you land on a spoofed login page.

Strong antivirus software can add another layer of protection if you click a malicious search result. It may warn you about known phishing sites, block dangerous downloads and stop other threats before they reach your device. However, no security software can protect you if you willingly enter your banking credentials on a convincing fake site, so always check the web address first. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Set up alerts for activity such as withdrawals and new logins if your bank offers them. Then review unexpected activity immediately. The FBI recommends regularly monitoring financial accounts for unauthorized transactions.

Identity theft protection can help monitor for signs that your personal information is being misused. Some services can alert you to suspicious activity involving your credit, financial accounts or personal information and provide recovery assistance if fraud occurs. This will not stop a fake bank ad, but it can give you another way to spot trouble after your information has been exposed. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com

If you think you entered your credentials on a fake banking page, contact your financial institution immediately using a number you trust. Then reset the exposed credentials. If you reused the same password on another account, change it there as well. The FBI also recommends reporting fraudulent wire transfers to the Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.gov. Acting quickly may improve the chances of stopping or reversing a transfer.
Kurt's key takeaways

What gets me about this scam is how normal the first step feels. You want to check your balance, so you search for your bank and choose a result that appears legitimate. There may be no strange email waiting in your inbox. You did not respond to an unexpected text. You started the search yourself. That can make the trap much harder to recognize. For banking, I would skip search results altogether. Use your bank's official app or a bookmark you have already verified. Then take a moment to look at the address before entering anything sensitive. A few extra seconds can be a lot easier than trying to recover money after it has left your account.

title: Electric Mercedes motorhome targets 621-mile range
summary: The Mercedes-Benz eActros 600 electric truck targets 621 miles per charge on a 28,000-mile round-the-world journey through over 30 countries.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

If you think you've seen some wild RVs, this one may reset the scale. Professional truck driver and content creator Tobias Wagner, better known online as Elektrotrucker, is preparing to drive around the world in a specially converted Mercedes-Benz eActros 600. A full Bliss Mobil living module sits behind the cab, turning this electric truck into a rolling home. Wagner plans to make the entire journey on battery power.

Mercedes-Benz Trucks says the route will cover about 28,000 miles through more than 30 countries over roughly one year, with a goal of no more than 80 charging stops. According to Mercedes, the trip would be the first known circumnavigation of the globe in a fully battery-electric truck. What really caught my attention is how far Wagner hopes to go between those stops. Here's how this massive electric motorhome works and why its 621-mile range target could be the toughest part of the trip.
100 KODIAK DRIVERLESS TRUCKS ARE HEADED FOR PUBLIC ROADS

A custom electric Mercedes-Benz eActros 600 motorhome is preparing for a 28,000-mile journey through more than 30 countries, testing the limits of long-range EV travel. (Tobias Wagner/Mercedes-Benz Trucks)
NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, September 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.
Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com
This electric Mercedes motorhome started as a long-haul truck

Underneath the living quarters sits the Mercedes-Benz eActros 600, a battery-electric truck built for long-distance commercial freight. Its three lithium iron phosphate battery packs provide a combined installed capacity of 621 kWh. Mercedes normally designs the truck to travel about 310 miles under specific fully loaded long-haul test conditions.

Wagner's expedition truck has a very different job. Instead of pulling a heavily loaded commercial trailer, it carries a custom living module. Mercedes also modified the truck with single rear tires and expedition equipment. Those changes help reduce weight and rolling resistance compared with a traditional freight configuration.

The finished expedition vehicle reportedly has a maximum weight of about 34,170 pounds. Power comes from Mercedes' electric axle and four-speed transmission. The eActros 600 produces about 536 horsepower continuously, with peak output reaching roughly 805 horsepower. That's a lot of muscle for a vehicle carrying its own kitchen and bed.
Could it really travel 621 miles on one charge?

This is where the project gets especially interesting. Wagner and Mercedes believe the lighter expedition setup, combined with careful hypermiling, could potentially travel as far as 621 miles on a single charge. That would be roughly double the range Mercedes quotes for a fully loaded eActros 600. Mercedes says the lighter expedition vehicle should significantly exceed the eActros 600's normal long-haul range. How close he gets will depend on road conditions, temperature, speed and terrain.
Why the 621-mile target could become important

Wagner wants to travel about 28,000 miles while stopping to charge no more than 80 times. That works out to an average of roughly 350 miles of driving per charging stop, although the actual distances will vary considerably along the route. Some stretches could become much more challenging.

The expedition will cross regions where high-powered truck charging remains difficult to find. The latest route includes Central and East Asia, Australia, the United States and several countries in Latin America. That's where stretching the truck well beyond its normal freight range could become useful.
ROBOTAXI PIT STOPS COULD POP UP NEAR YOU

Professional driver Tobias Wagner plans to circle the globe in a one-off electric expedition truck, aiming to complete the trip with no more than 80 charging stops. (Tobias Wagner/Mercedes-Benz Trucks)
Charging a 621-kWh battery takes serious power

Eventually, even this giant battery has to plug in. The eActros 600 supports CCS2 fast charging at up to 400 kW. Mercedes says that level of charging can take the battery from 10% to 80% in about 70 minutes under its specified conditions. Mercedes has also demonstrated Megawatt Charging System technology at up to 1,000 kW, which can cut charging times dramatically on compatible equipment.

Wagner's expedition setup has also been prepared for different charging systems around the world. It includes charging connections positioned on both sides of the truck. The project also has adapters designed for charging infrastructure in China and North America. That flexibility could prove essential once the truck leaves Europe. Mercedes revealed another important backup. Wagner has equipped the truck with his own Alpitronic DC charging station. That lets him charge from AC connections at up to 43 kW in special situations when conventional high-powered truck charging is not available.
The back of the truck is a fully electric home

Bliss Mobil added a roughly 13-foot expedition module behind the cab. Inside, Wagner gets a U-shaped dining area along with a kitchen. A bathroom sits toward the rear. There's also a drop-down bed that stores above the dining area when he wants more room during the day. The camper can sleep as many as four people. Wagner will have considerably more room because his primary travel companion is his dog, Krümelix.

The living module also follows the electric theme. It uses a separate 400-Ah lithium battery supported by 1,000 watts of solar power. That system handles equipment such as the induction cooktop, refrigerator and air conditioning. It also powers other onboard systems without relying on diesel or propane. The motorhome reportedly carries about 106 gallons of fresh water. A multistage filtration system helps Wagner manage water during extended stretches away from traditional campgrounds.
The camper can operate separately from the truck

Bliss Mobil designed the expedition module as a largely self-contained unit. Its electrical and plumbing systems sit within the camper rather than depending on the truck itself. That approach allows Bliss Mobil modules to move between compatible truck chassis.

Wagner's module does have a 24-volt connection to the eActros. That means the living area can draw energy from the truck's main battery when necessary. Still, the expedition has an obvious reason to conserve that electricity. Every bit of power used inside the camper could otherwise help move a nearly 17-ton vehicle farther down the road.
There's an electric motorcycle riding on the back

A giant expedition truck can handle plenty of roads, but there will always be places where its size becomes a problem. Wagner has another electric solution for that. A motorcycle carrier on the back holds a Honda WN7 electric motorcycle. When the road becomes too tight for the eActros, Wagner can leave the motorhome behind and continue on two wheels. The motorcycle uses a 9.3-kWh battery and produces about 67 horsepower. It's a useful backup for a trip designed to reach places far beyond normal highway rest stops.
TOYOTA JOINS HYDROGEN TRUCK ALLIANCE PUSH
Mercedes-Benz says the converted eActros 600 could travel as far as 621 miles on a charge under ideal conditions, though real-world results will vary. (Tobias Wagner/Mercedes-Benz Trucks)
Nearly $800,000 buys one very unusual motorhome

None of this comes cheaply. A price sheet displayed with the vehicle broke down the cost of the eActros 600 truck, Bliss Mobil camper and additional equipment. The total is approximately $796,600 including tax based on the exchange rate used at the time. Call it nearly $800,000. The Honda electric motorcycle wasn't included in that figure.

Of course, this also isn't a production RV you can configure at your local Mercedes dealership. Wagner's vehicle is a specialized one-off expedition build created around a commercial electric truck. We've seen other companies rethink how electric vehicles fit into camping. The CyberTrailer takes a different approach, using solar power and an onboard energy system to support off-grid travel.
The around-the-world trip starts Sept. 20

Mercedes-Benz Trucks says Wagner will officially depart from IAA Transportation 2026 in Hanover, Germany, on Sunday, Sept. 20. From there, the trip is expected to last about a year. Mercedes says Wagner will travel through around 30 countries on five continents while putting battery-electric truck technology through real-world conditions well beyond familiar European freight routes. Mercedes says the planned route may still change as the trip progresses. The vehicle may be built for an extraordinary adventure, but the results could tell us something much bigger about electric transportation.
What this means to you

You probably won't be putting an $800,000 electric expedition truck in your driveway. Still, this trip could answer questions that eventually affect far more ordinary electric vehicles. Range is only part of the EV equation. Reliable charging becomes even more important when you leave major highways or travel through areas with limited infrastructure. Wagner will be testing both. If the eActros can consistently travel well beyond its standard commercial range, engineers will get another example of how vehicle weight and driving technique can change battery performance.

The charging side may prove equally revealing. A vehicle can carry an enormous battery, but long-distance travel still depends on finding equipment powerful enough to recharge it. Wagner's onboard charging equipment gives him another option when high-powered public chargers are unavailable, but slower charging could add considerable time to the trip.

We have already seen experiments that attack the charging problem from another direction. One electric road project is testing technology that can transfer power to vehicles while they drive. Wagner's trip takes the opposite approach. He is bringing a huge battery and finding out how far today's infrastructure can take it.
Kurt's key takeaways

I love a good road trip, but this one takes the idea to another level. What fascinates me most isn't simply whether Wagner can squeeze 621 miles out of this massive battery. I want to see what happens when he leaves the easy charging routes behind and has to make this technology work across more than 30 countries. That's where this trip could get really interesting. A giant battery and impressive range numbers are great, but you still need a working charger when you pull in. If Wagner can circle the globe with roughly 80 charging stops, that's a pretty strong demonstration of how far electric trucking has come. And if he gets stranded looking for power along the way, we'll learn something from that, too.

title: Can tech really get you off your phone and into real life?
summary: NewTree Social founder Maddy O'Connor built a community events app to help people discover local gatherings, wellness events and run clubs nearby.
story: Kendall Schrohe, co-founder of AttentionSphere.org, discusses how young Americans are participating in a one-month digital detox challenge, swapping smartphones for flip phones.
How many times have you picked up your phone to check one thing and found yourself still scrolling 30 minutes later? I know I've done it.

Our phones make it incredibly easy to stay connected. Yet something interesting seems to be happening at the same time. Many people are looking for more reasons to put those phones down and spend time with other people in the real world.
Run clubs are growing. Local gatherings are drawing attention. Phone-free events are popping up. People seem hungry for experiences that feel a little less like another feed.

That raises an interesting question: Could the same technology that keeps pulling us online also help get us back into real life? That idea is behind NewTree Social, an early-stage community events app from 29-year-old founder Maddy O'Connor. She wants people to use their phones to discover something happening nearby, make a plan and then go experience it. And the timing may be right.
RESTAURANTS BAN DINERS' PHONES DURING MEALS AS NO-SCROLL TREND GROWS: PUT IT AWAY OR ELSE
More people are looking for ways to put their phones down, step away from the screen and spend more time connecting in the real world. (iStock)
NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, September 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.
Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com.
More people are looking beyond the screen

There is some real data behind this shift. Eventbrite's 2026 Social Study surveyed people ages 18 to 35 in the U.S. and U.K. It found that 79% planned to attend more events in 2026. Among Gen Z respondents, 46% said they were limiting screen time and 74% said in-person experiences were more important than digital ones.
Now, keep in mind that this research comes from Eventbrite, a company whose business revolves around live events. Still, those numbers line up with something we are seeing play out in the real world.

Eventbrite says phone-free experiences listed on its platform grew 567% globally between 2024 and 2025. Attendance at those events rose 121%. The company based those numbers on events that used "phone-free" terminology in their title or description.

For people who have spent years with a smartphone within arm's reach, intentionally putting it away feels significant. It also creates an unusual opening for technology. Instead of asking how an app can keep you scrolling longer, what if the goal becomes helping you find something worth closing the app for?
One young founder saw an opportunity

That is where O'Connor comes in. She told CyberGuy that the idea for NewTree grew partly from her own experience living in Washington, D.C., without an established group of friends. Her experience changed depending on where she lived and whether she could find places where meeting new people felt natural.
At the same time, she was watching interest grow around run clubs, wellness events, social clubs and other in-person experiences. So she started building around that behavior.
NewTree is designed to help people discover local activities and meet others through something they already want to do. I think that part is important.

Walking into a room of strangers solely because you are supposed to meet people can feel awkward. Walking into a fitness class, community event or gathering you already find interesting gives you a reason to be there before you ever introduce yourself. For someone who recently moved or simply wants to expand a social circle, that could make taking the first step a little easier.
NewTree wants your scrolling to lead somewhere
Open NewTree and the basic experience should feel familiar. There is a feed. You browse events nearby. You can RSVP and get reminders about something you want to attend.

But the idea behind that feed is a little different. O'Connor comes from a graphic design background and told CyberGuy that she deliberately wanted NewTree to feel more like a social platform than a traditional events directory.
The app currently focuses on community, fitness and wellness events around Tampa, St. Pete and Clearwater. Apple describes it as an app for discovering local events, RSVPing and meeting new people.

Hosts can add photos and videos to event listings. Users can browse what is happening around them and RSVP from their phones. O'Connor also wants reviews to play a bigger role in what people discover. She says reviews of a host's events can affect how those events perform in the feed instead of simply sitting on a profile.
There is something almost funny about the concept. You open another social-style app because you want to spend less of your social life inside apps. But maybe that is exactly the point.
EXPERTS REVEAL WHY 'NONNAMAXXING' TREND MAY IMPROVE MENTAL, PHYSICAL HEALTH
NewTree Social founder Maddy O'Connor is shown with the app, which she created to help people discover local events and spend more time connecting in person. (NewTree)
How NewTree says it is different
NewTree is entering a crowded space. Meetup, Eventbrite and Facebook already help people discover events nearby, and both Meetup and Eventbrite offer personalized recommendations.

So what is NewTree trying to do differently? O'Connor says she wants the experience to feel more like a social platform built specifically around getting people together in person. She also says reviews can influence how a host's events perform in the feed, so better-reviewed experiences can potentially receive greater visibility. During NewTree's early pilot, O'Connor is personally reviewing and approving hosts before their events can appear publicly.

None of those ideas completely reinvents event discovery. The bet is that putting them together in a more curated, community-focused experience will give people another useful way to find things to do and meet people nearby. Whether that gives people enough reason to add NewTree to the apps they already use is one of the biggest things the company still has to prove.
The real test starts after you close the app

Here is what I would be watching. Does NewTree help people make plans they actually follow through on? Getting someone to download an app is one thing. Getting them to put on shoes, leave home and show up somewhere is much harder.
The idea works if you spend a few minutes browsing NewTree, find something interesting and eventually put the phone back in your pocket because you have somewhere to go.
It becomes a lot less interesting if people simply scroll through another feed filled with things they might someday do. O'Connor is very open about just how early NewTree is.

She told CyberGuy that NewTree is pre-traction and pre-revenue. Tampa Bay is the starting point because she wants to prove that people will use the platform in one market before trying to expand throughout Florida and eventually nationwide. So there is a long way to go. But the behavior NewTree is betting on already appears to be taking shape.
Safety has to follow you into the real world

Of course, using an app to find events where you may meet strangers brings some very real safety questions. O'Connor says she has taken a hands-on approach during NewTree's MVP stage. She told CyberGuy that she personally reviews and approves hosts before their events can appear on the platform. Users can report content or other users and block people. Hosts can also remove or report attendees.

NewTree's current support page says business profiles are reviewed before they can post. However, there is an important limitation. A verified badge means NewTree says it has confirmed that the business is who it claims to be. It does not mean NewTree is endorsing or guaranteeing a specific event.

NewTree's terms go further. They say events are generally operated independently by outside hosts and that NewTree does not ordinarily perform criminal background checks or identity verification on users, attendees, hosts or organizers.

So I would still do some homework before showing up at an unfamiliar event. Look up the organizer independently. Check the venue. If you are uncomfortable going alone, bring someone you trust. Technology can help you find people. It cannot remove all of the risks that come with meeting people you do not know.
What happens to your location?

Privacy deserves a close look too. O'Connor told CyberGuy that NewTree collects basic account information, including your name, email, date of birth and location. She says the app can use a saved profile location or, with your permission, your device location.

She also said the information is stored through NewTree's Supabase database, with database-level access controls designed to limit who can access different information. When someone RSVPs to a free event, O'Connor says the host receives the attendee's name, email and location information so they can manage and communicate with attendees.
1 IN 6 ADULTS PLAGUED BY LONELINESS AS RESEARCHERS REVEAL LASTING IMPACT OF COVID PANDEMIC
The NewTree app lets users browse nearby events, view host profiles and RSVP to activities that interest them. (NewTree)
There is also an age-rating wrinkle
Another detail could cause some confusion. Apple currently gives NewTree a 13+ age rating. NewTree itself says you must be at least 18 years old to create an account or use the platform.

O'Connor told CyberGuy that Apple's 13+ label reflects its content-based App Store rating rather than the minimum age NewTree allows on the platform. So, despite what you may see on the App Store listing, NewTree says the service itself is for adults 18 and older.
NewTree still has plenty to prove
Right now, Apple lists NewTree as an iPhone app. O'Connor told CyberGuy that Android support is planned but not available yet.

The business model is still taking shape too. O'Connor says she is leaning toward keeping the app free for users while eventually offering optional premium tools for businesses and hosts. Exactly what those paid features would include has not been decided.
So I would look at NewTree for what it is today: a very early app built around a much larger change in the way some people are thinking about technology.
What this means to you

Most of us could probably use a few more reasons to put the phone down and do something in the real world. Our phones have become where we communicate, work, watch videos and fill just about every empty moment.
Sometimes the screen starts taking the place of the experiences it was supposed to help us find. Maybe the better approach is expecting more from the technology we already use.

If an app helps you discover a local event, try something you would never have considered or meet someone you otherwise never would have crossed paths with, the phone becomes the starting point. Then it can get out of the way.
I like that idea. Use the technology to find something worth doing. Then look up from the screen and go do it.
Kurt's key takeaways

What stands out to me here is how good technology has become at keeping us looking down. Notifications pull us back in. Feeds always have something else waiting. Before you know it, another chunk of your day has disappeared into a screen. Now we are seeing signs that many people want something different. They still want technology, but they also want more opportunities to be around people in the real world. NewTree has a lot to prove. But I like the problem O'Connor is trying to solve. Your phone already knows how to keep you home and entertained for hours. Maybe the next really useful social app will be the one that gives you a good reason to leave.
Would you use an app designed to get you off your phone and out meeting people, or does downloading another social app defeat the whole purpose? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.
