Rodan-Benzaquen says of European Jews, "electorally, we don't weigh," so they have again become a political football. She says when left and far-left parties say, "Oh, we want to fight against antisemitism. The only reason why they're saying it is because it's a tool to attack the far-right."

Tyler Speicher is an American journalist living in Slovenia after spending 25 years covering stories ranging from the Little League World Series to hurricanes, 9/11 and its aftermath for New York City news outlets, including 20 years on the Fox News Channel assignment desk.

title: Elon Musk is flying under the radar in the Texas Senate race. Republicans like it that way.
summary: The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 state Supreme Court race in Wisconsin.
story: The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 state Supreme Court race in Wisconsin. He donned an oversized cheese hat, offered $1 million checks to voters, and he and affiliated groups poured at least $20 million into the contest.
In the end, the conservative candidate lost by 10 points in what was widely viewed as a rebuke of Musk and the Trump administration.

Now, the richest person in the world is back boosting Republican candidates in critical midterm elections, including a bruising Senate race in Texas where Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democrat James Talarico, who had initially far outraised him and remains close in polling.
But that financial tide is quickly turning — with Musk’s help.

Unlike in Wisconsin, Musk has so far stayed out of the spotlight in Texas, even though he lives in the state, has based his companies Tesla and SpaceX there, and employs about 20,000 people. He hasn’t announced plans for any in-person events, or teased — as he did in Wisconsin — that he’d be handing out $1 million checks to voters.

Privately, Republicans say they want Musk to keep his distance. In interviews, more than half a dozen Republican strategists involved in the Texas Senate race say they hope Musk follows his 2024 model of electoral involvement, which led to a Republican sweep of the White House and Congress. Then, Musk spent more than $250 million on Donald Trump and his party.

Republicans believe Democrats will attempt to turn Musk into a boogeyman if he takes on a higher-profile role in Texas or other battlegrounds. One Republican consultant involved in the Texas Senate race said that was the perception in Wisconsin.

“He came in super late, and it was very public,” said the consultant, who, like others interviewed for this article, were granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Elon spending money became the story, which I think maybe was a mistake.”
A different Republican strategist involved in Texas campaigns said those around Musk learned from the experience.
“Did Elon bring some things to the Wisconsin race that hampered things? Probably,” the person added. “But I think they will adjust for that.”
Add to Google
Add to Google
Democrats, however, say they welcome Musk more publicly entering the fray in Texas.

“Elon, bring it. You’ve failed in Wisconsin. You’ll fail in Texas,” said Nathan Johnson, a Democrat running to replace Paxton as attorney general. “I’m not afraid of Elon bringing his political money here. All these policies favor him or people like him.”

An in-your-face Musk campaign would play into Talarico’s narrative that the real American divide isn’t left versus right but “top versus bottom,” with elites and billionaires exerting control over the working class, they say.

“James is running largely on costs and corruption,” Luke Warford, a Texas-based Democratic strategist and chair of the Travis County Democratic Party, said of Talarico. “The idea of the richest man in the world coming in late to try to buy the election and save Ken Paxton really plays into James Talarico’s argument.”

The Texas Senate race has all the makings of a contest that would attract Musk. The conservative narrative building against Talarico amplifies his past remarks in support of transgender people, including his comment that “God is nonbinary.” Talarico told Fox News he was being “provocative” and was trying to convey that one cannot use “human categories to define God.”

Musk has spoken publicly about his own transgender daughter, Vivian Jenna Wilson, saying she was “not a girl” and was figuratively “dead.” He also alleged that he had been “tricked” into authorizing trans-related medical treatment for her when she was 16. Wilson previously told NBC News that Musk was an absent father who was cruel to her as a child for being queer and feminine.

At this point, Musk’s America PAC has not said how much it will invest in Texas, but a person with knowledge of the group’s thinking indicated that as of now, the Paxton-Talarico contest was not slotted to receive more focus than other Senate or congressional races the group is investing in across the country, saying “every state and district where we are spending is a priority.”
To date, America PAC has spent nearly $5.2 million on digital ads, mail, live calls and pamphleting in Texas, but that number is expected to significantly climb.

In all, the super PAC has spent $14.7 million on congressional races, including seven Senate races and nearly three dozen House races. The group has spent the most money on the Texas Senate race, followed by nearly $3 million on Senate races in Ohio and Michigan.

National Republican groups long knew they would have to provide air cover for Paxton because of an initial fundraising disadvantage to Talarico, who had $21 million in cash on hand compared to Paxton’s $1.7 million at the end of June, according to campaign finance reports. Today, a flood of Republican money is pouring in from several sources and the balance has suddenly tipped in Paxton’s favor.

“America PAC is working in full coordination with the entire GOP apparatus and is investing in the states and districts that will decide control of the House and Senate,” America PAC spokesman Andrew Romeo said in a statement. “Our only priority is ensuring Republicans keep full control of Washington and stopping the lunatic left from bringing us back to the days of open borders, rampant crime, and woke policies.”

Paxton’s status as a scandal-plagued candidate who has been impeached and indicted — coupled with the fact he’s coming off a contentious primary against Sen. John Cornyn and much of the Republican Party establishment, aside from Trump — makes him among the most vulnerable front-line Senate Republican candidates in a state where Democrats have not won a statewide post in three decades.

After Trump’s late endorsement helped propel Paxton over Cornyn, groups like the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, were left scrambling. The election cycle budgets were, in part, built on the idea that Cornyn would not need nearly as much national fundraising help.

“Cornyn had his own fundraising machine, he could raise a lot of money on his own, so it was going to make things easier to cover other important close races,” said a Republican consultant familiar with the thought process. “I know they [Elon] are focused more on the ground game stuff. MAGA Inc. is on digital and mail. This pretty much turned out the way we thought it would. It’s an expensive endeavor and a team and multigroup effort.”
The pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC has pumped at least $15 million into TV ads that have included hitting Talarico on previous votes involving China.
So far, MAGA Inc. has spent $10 million in the state to help boost Paxton, its second-biggest single-state investment.

The group did not return a request for comment, but in an interview with NBC News last week, MAGA Inc. chief James Blair said the group had booked $10 million worth of TV ad time in Texas. Blair noted the previous disparity in spending, with Talarico and related groups pummeling Paxton on TV.

“The fact is Ken Paxton had $100 million spent against him in the primary,” Blair said. “Talarico had $0 spent against him in the primary, and that has an impact on candidate images that takes time to rectify. But the resources … have begun to be deployed now in earnest [and] will take care of that problem.”
A veteran GOP official directly involved in the race contended that the shift toward spending in Texas did not take away from other battlegrounds.

“This spending will not take away from other investments,” the official said. “This came from a collection of Texas folks very committed to making sure that seat remains Republican. They see the polling, and that James Talarico is so extreme. No one wants to see Texas turn blue.”

When asked about the onslaught of money headed toward Talarico, spokesman JT Ennis said, “Billionaire-backed dark money groups are lying about James because they’re scared of the people-powered movement we’re building to fix this broken, corrupt political system.”

title: Poll: Most voters say Trump has hurt the economy as competitive midterm election looms
summary: President Donald Trump’s sinking ratings threaten to drag down Republicans in November’s midterm elections, as voters blame him for high prices and a shaky economy, according to a new NBC News poll.
story: President Donald Trump’s sinking ratings threaten to drag down Republicans in November’s midterm elections, as voters blame him for high prices and a shaky economy, according to a new NBC News poll.

The president’s approval rating stands at 41% among registered voters, a second-term low in the poll, with a majority (55%) of voters saying they believe Trump’s policies have hurt the economy. That’s up from 48% in March, before the Iran war pushed up prices on gas and other goods and cemented the rising cost of living as voters’ most pressing issue.

title: Tehran warns of ‘new weapons’ as Trump weighs meeting with Iranian president
summary: Iran warned Monday it would use “new weapons with new capabilities” if the U.S. launched a fresh assault after President Donald Trump ramped up the rhetoric against Tehran over the weekend.
story: Iran warned Monday it would use “new weapons with new capabilities” if the U.S. launched a fresh assault after President Donald Trump ramped up the rhetoric against Tehran over the weekend.

“If a new aggression takes place, we will definitely change the weapons and geography of the war,” Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Monday, according to the semiofficial Fars news agency.
Mohebbi did not provide details on what the new weapons were or which new locations could be hit.

Earlier, Trump said he would “probably” be open to meeting with his Iranian counterpart, President Masoud Pezeshkian, during the United Nations General Assembly this week, Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reported Sunday.

The possibility of a meeting offered a glimmer of hope for a resolution to the nearly seven-month war with Iran, which has resulted in Iran blocking the key Strait of Hormuz, and its Yemeni allies bombing a crucial east-west oil pipeline and threatening another crucial waterway. Resultant economic shock waves have hit the U.S. and the world economy, driving up oil and diesel prices and fueling inflation.

title: The Chiefs and Patrick Mahomes look like their old selves, but now with new help
summary: With playmakers surrounding Patrick Mahomes, and late-game moxie that helped them survive a wild overtime play, the Kansas City Chiefs improved to 2-0.
story: The Kansas City Chiefs last season lost more than Patrick Mahomes, their franchise cornerstone player, to a season-ending injury.

Well before the star quarterback injured two ligaments in his left knee last December, the Chiefs had already lost the air of invincibility they’d built while becoming the NFL’s most-feared team in close games.

That quality had earned the Chiefs three Super Bowl titles under coach Andy Reid, and a 17-game winning streak in games decided by 8 points or less. That streak was snapped in last year’s first game, and from there only got worse.

By last season’s end, their record in one-score games was 1-9, a turnaround some attributed to Mahomes’ inconsistent play before his injury, or a supporting cast of receivers and running backs had grown thin. Tight end Travis Kelce, one of the most prolific pass-catchers in the position’s history, was in the middle of one of his worst statistical seasons. On the ground, the Chiefs ranked near the league’s bottom third in yards per carry.
But two games into this new season, Kansas City is 2-0 and again looks like a team that could be feared in the AFC.

Mahomes appears uninhibited by his knee injury, and now has a number of playmakers surrounding him — led by a familiar face, and one new. And in Sunday’s 33-30 overtime win against Indianapolis, the Chiefs showed again they know how to win a close game while overcoming a wild play that might have changed the outcome.
“There was never a doubt that we were going to get that win,” Kelce said.

A walk-off 40-yard field goal as time expired by Harrison Butker gave the Chiefs their eighth consecutive overtime win in the regular season, tying an NFL record also held by San Francisco (2003-10). Mahomes, who threw for 382 yards and three touchdowns, now has 25 career game-winning drives in the fourth quarter or overtime. The Chiefs join Las Vegas, Cincinnati and Buffalo as the only remaining undefeated teams in the AFC.
“That’s what this NFL is about is just finding a way to win games,” Mahomes said on NBC’s “Sunday Night Football.”
Kansas City thought it had the game won with five minutes remaining in overtime.

Tied at 30-30, Colts quarterback Daniel Jones connected with Laquon Treadwell for a 48-yard gain down to Kansas City’s 17-yard line when Treadwell bobbled and recovered the catch while evading one tackle by L’Jarius Sneed. Trying to gain more yardage, Treadwell was then tackled by Chiefs cornerback Nohl Williams, who punched the ball out for a fumble recovered by Kansas City. Under regular-season overtime rules that have been in place since 2025 that allow each team at least one possession each, Kansas City believed it had won the game by forcing a turnover and stopping the Colts short of tying the game on its first overtime drive.

An official review, however, found that Sneed’s left hand grazed the right hip of Treadwell at the same time he secured his bobbled catch — a brush of a few fingers that was barely enough to count Treadwell as down by contact, however slight, at that moment. It negated the fumble that followed. The Colts were still alive.

A touchdown would win the game for Indianapolis, but three plays later it still wasn’t close to the end zone. On fourth and 8, 15 yards from a score, the Colts put their offense on the field and looked ready to snap if they had seen the defense they wanted. When they didn’t, the Colts kicked the field goal for a 30-30 tie. By doing so, Mahomes was left with plenty of time to mount a comeback.
“Had a play called,” Colts coach Shane Steichen said of the fourth-down decision. “Had to love the look to run it there.”

Mahomes jogged into the huddle with 3:06 remaining in overtime knowing the next score would win. He and the Chiefs made it a reality by turning to the franchise’s newest weapon, Kenneth Walker, the Most Valuable Player of last February’s Super Bowl for Seattle who became the team’s prized offseason signing as a free agent.
Walker rushed the ball three times for 18 yards, caught a 22-yard pass from Mahomes, and rushed two more yards to set up Butker’s game-winning kick.

One week after producing a career-high 191 yards from scrimmage during his Chiefs debut in Week 1, a total helped by Walker’s league-best 14 broken tackles, he finished with 117 rushing yards on 24 carries and added 61 yards receiving against the Colts. Walker has looked every bit the missing piece capable of taking pressure off of Mahomes on the ground and opening up the passing game.

“We able to, I guess, freestyle it,” Walker told NBC in a postgame interview of his connection with Mahomes. “If I’m open or if somebody open, play break down, he able to make plays, so it’s great to play with him.”

Even more encouraging for Kansas City was not just how quickly a new addition in Walker has integrated into the offense, but how much Kelce — the record-breaking tight end who helped jump-start the team’s dynasty alongside Mahomes — resembled his old self Sunday.

Kelce has debated whether to retire each of the last two offseasons after producing career-low yardage totals and just eight touchdowns combined in 2024-25. He was targeted on fewer than seven passes per game last season.

On Sunday, a faster, more agile Kelce was targeted 11 times, more than any Chiefs pass-catcher. He caught nine passes for 101 yards including a touchdown that left his pop superstar wife, Taylor Swift, pointing to her wedding ring in a suite in celebration. It was his first game with 100-plus yards and a touchdown since Week 7 of 2023. Kelce now has 128 yards after contact this season, the most in his career through a season’s first two games, per ESPN.
“We’re in a zone right now where everybody’s feeding off each other and it’s only making us better and it’s making us play harder for each other.”

The contributions from Mahomes and his co-stars, and the team’s late-game moxie, have kept the Chiefs undefeated. Still to be seen is whether those factors also can reverse a troubling trend over the course of a long season. Between 2017-22, the Chiefs ranked among the league’s 10 best in scoring every season and led the NFL in points in 2018 and 2022. In the last three years, though, they ranked 15th in both 2023 and 2024 before dropping to 21st last season.
“The parity in this league is crazy,” Chiefs coach Reid said. “You’re going to have some once-score games. You have to bear down, and our guys did that.”

title: What might an AI doomsday look like? Experts have given it some thought
summary: A small but dedicated group of AI experts has been warning for years that increasingly powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic damage or even lead to human extinction.
story: A small but dedicated group of AI experts has been warning for years that increasingly powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic damage or even lead to human extinction. Now, an explosion of interest worldwide has magnified long-simmering questions about how exactly an AI doomsday scenario could materialize.

In interviews, AI researchers, analysts studying the intersection of AI and the military, and biologists studying AI-mediated risks said that worries about the technology’s growing capabilities are not the stuff of science fiction. Instead, they said, humans acting alone or with state support could soon use AI systems to cause potentially catastrophic harm.

AI safety researchers also predict that self-improving AI systems — which AI leaders say could emerge in the coming years — could coordinate complex influence campaigns to gain control of military systems and execute a coup against human governments.
And those are just the scenarios experts can currently envision.

Peter Barnett, a technical AI researcher at the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), a California-based nonprofit dedicated to preventing human extinction from artificial superintelligence, said “there are many ways in which this could go very badly and result in everyone dead.”

“If the AI is smarter than all humans, it will likely be able to find and act on attack vectors that humans didn’t think of,” Barnett said, arguing that AI systems capable of autonomously improving themselves pose the most significant risks for humanity.

Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta all recently disclosed that AI systems have already disobeyed human developers’ instructions — in some cases autonomously hacking third-party companies, leading to growing concerns internally and from the general public — and causing some researchers at the companies to quit to focus on safety efforts.

Though many AI researchers working at the technology’s cutting edge have expressed these existential fears — both in interviews with NBC News and in a flurry of social media posts last week — many hesitate to say which specific pathway could cause the most harm to humans.

Over a dozen AI company employees told NBC News they are frightened by the overall direction of the industry, without fully knowing which vector may pose the most risk. Others have spoken out publicly.
Add to Google
Add to Google

“If you go to play a game of chess against Magnus Carlsen, I predict you will lose,” said Nate Soares, the president of MIRI and a longtime AI critic, on “The Tucker Carlson Show” this week. “If you then ask, ‘What piece will he use to checkmate me?’ that’s a much harder question.”
Despite the uncertainty, researchers in the AI world have attempted to make concrete predictions about some of the more plausible scenarios for AI-fueled disaster.

One prominent AI safety organization, the California-based Center for AI Safety, created an online textbook in early 2024 to break the scenarios into four key categories: rogue AIs, malicious use, AI race dynamics and organizational risks.

The specter of rogue AI systems marauding the internet, perhaps seizing control of critical infrastructure like energy grids or water facilities, became concrete in July, when fleets of AI agents from OpenAI illicitly gained access to the internet, hacked into an external company and colluded to cover their tracks — all without the knowledge of OpenAI’s staff.
Many AI experts fear that these sorts of rogue AI behaviors will only increase once systems are able to improve themselves autonomously — often referred to as “recursive self-improvement.”

Jeffrey Ladish, the executive director of Palisade Research, an AI advocacy and research organization, said many of his contacts at leading AI companies were surprised and shaken by July’s autonomous cyberattack. The attack caused researchers to worry that self-improving AI systems might emerge sooner than expected.
“AI researchers are now like, “Oh, s---, recursive self-improvement. That’s really going to happen now,” Ladish said. “That’s terrifying.”
Barnett, of MIRI, said self-improving, smarter-than-human AI systems could quickly gain political influence and convince military and political leaders to delegate more authority to AI systems.

“Government officials might have attempted to install ‘kill switches’ that could disable a rogue system, but the AI is superhuman at hacking and would be able to disable the kill switch,” Barnett said. “This leaves the AI in a perfect position to literally coup the government.” After that, Barnett said, it would be trivial for an AI system to kill civilians who impede the AI’s goals or progress.
Gov. Shapiro says U.S. should ‘listen to the people’ building AI

On Friday, California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced a new executive order establishing an expert task force to, among other aims, formulate recommendations targeting “the creation of an AI kill switch.”
Several of the researchers who spoke to NBC News said that humans could leverage AI systems to inflict cataclysmic damage well before recursive self-improvement materializes.

As an example of how AI systems could be harnessed by humans for malicious use, experts posit that AI could supercharge the ability to synthesize potent biological or chemical weapons, potentially creating the opportunity to unleash pathogens many times more lethal than the Covid-19 virus.

“For biorisk, we should be worried now,” said Jake Jordan, vice president of global biological policy and programs at the Washington, D.C.-based Nuclear Threat Initiative. Jordan said that AI systems can already help bad actors design dangerous biological materials, such as proteins that evade detection tools used to screen for harmful substances, pointing to research published by Microsoft in October.

Jordan also noted that AI can be used beyond the biological design process. “If you develop a pathway to produce some sort of pathogen, AI might be useful in helping with the production,” Jordan said, in addition to disseminating the bioweapon or scaling its impact.

Just last week, Anthropic released a lengthy report saying users outside of the U.S. attempted to use the company’s AI systems to perform risky biological research. The company said one researcher exchanged thousands of messages with its AI systems about improving the mammalian transmission of a highly lethal bird flu virus.

“There are some very, very easy-to-ask questions that could conceivably be very innocuous but could lead you down very useful routes if you were trying to really enhance the scale of harm,” Jordan said.

Beyond biology, experts posit that politicians or military leaders could attempt to adopt AI as fast as possible, despite safety risks, for fear that other countries would do the same and create more powerful AI-fueled military tools.

This transformation is already underway: In January, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced his intention to transform the country’s military into an “AI-first” force, while China’s military also views AI as imperative for future warfare. At the same time, drones “guided entirely by AI” killed civilians in Ukraine several months ago. Last week, the Pentagon’s former head of AI said it is “inevitable” that AI is used in systems adjacent to nuclear weapon command systems, addressing fears that AI systems could be involved in the launch of nuclear weapons.

Hamza Chaudhry, the AI and national security lead at the Future of Life Institute, a nonprofit organization dedicated to helping humanity navigate transformative technologies, pointed to AI’s swift adoption throughout the military, even while many military leaders express skepticism.

The Pentagon’s 2027 budget requests nearly $75 million to modernize and incorporate AI into systems that help commanders manage forces and make battlefield decisions. Chaudhry emphasized that the Pentagon’s budget proposal also requests significant funding to integrate AI into the software systems that undergird the military’s nuclear command and control structure.

“These AI systems continuously hallucinate, including in war-fighting settings,” he said, noting that an AI-fueled error in satellite detection networks or sensor systems could potentially lead to inadvertent escalation and nuclear launches. “These are scenarios that folks are seriously thinking about in D.C.,” he said.

Beyond biological and nuclear threats, AI companies face harsh organizational incentives to develop AI even faster and — experts say — more recklessly. Over the past year, AI leaders have admitted that the rate of technological development is too fast even for them. On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed a new effort to “pace the frontier” of AI, calling on all leading AI companies to advance at a deliberate speed so their internal efforts to test and monitor the systems can keep up with the models’ capabilities.
Add to Google
Add to Google

In January, Amodei and Google DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis agreed that they would ideally have more time to develop their products safely, but that organizational and market forces pushed them toward faster iteration.

Quicker AI development can mean that oversight teams within the leading AI companies have less time to ensure systems are safe. While OpenAI has a safety and security committee and teams of researchers dedicated to safety efforts, the company on Wednesday shared six new incidents in which it said its systems failed to follow human directions.

Worries about catastrophe are not universal in the AI industry — many experts working on AI policy, building AI applications or developing hardware see these sorts of fears as overblown, fearmongering or just detached from reality.

“I’m not scared of a terminator situation and I never have been,” said Keegan McBride, director of science and technology policy at the Tony Blair Institute, a British think tank that advises political leaders and governments. “Scientific progress has always defined humanity, and this is just the next step,” he said.
Others see the magnification of extinction worries as a purposeful distraction from immediate, real-world AI harms.

AI ethicist and computer scientist Timnit Gebru, a longtime skeptic of the hype generated by leading AI companies, wrote on LinkedIn this week that the latest firestorm was further evidence that these companies exaggerate their products’ power for their own gain. “Do you really want to regulate the industry for minor things like data center pollution issues or data theft or labor exploitation or plagiarism when you can risk China, not the U.S., having a machine god, they ask?”

Garrison Lovely, an AI expert and independent journalist who is about to publish a book on AI companies’ drive to render humans obsolete, said allusions to machine gods and extinction miss the larger point about AI’s trajectory. “I think that the AI safety community sometimes makes this mistake of thinking you need to prove the most extreme and difficult case,” Lovely said.
“Even building merely human-level AI that can replace human labor across the board,” he said. “That would be way too much.”

title: CNN, Politico and MS NOW plan to sue Trump admin over ban on White House coverage
summary: News outlets CNN, Politico and MS NOW filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration after President Donald Trump banned from covering the White House.
story: Media outlets CNN, Politico and MS NOW filed a lawsuit Monday against the Trump administration after President Donald Trump banned them from covering the White House.
The president announced the ban Friday on Truth Social, citing what he said was “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”

In a joint statement on social media, the three outlets said they notified the administration Monday that they were filing the suit “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.”

“Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting,” the statement continued. “Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.”

Reached for comment on the lawsuit, the White House press office directed NBC News to Trump’s Truth Social post defending the move Monday morning. In the post, the president called the ban “an assault” on the news media, which he claimed is “a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”
Trump has targeted journalists and outlets he dislikes, but the ban is the most extreme instance so far of the president’s push to hinder press access.

Secret Service members turned away reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House grounds and revoked their passes Saturday, prompting backlash from experts and the White House Correspondents’ Association, which called the move unconstitutional. CNN’s and MS NOW’s workspaces in the White House sat empty following their access being withdrawn.

The publications have long been part of the White House press pool, a group of media outlets that cover the president. The pool, which is managed by the White House Correspondents’ Association, assigns a small number of reporters each day to cover the president on behalf of the full press corps. The assigned outlet rotates. CNN, now banned, was assigned to pool duty Monday, providing broadcast coverage meant to be shared with all members of the press corps.
On Sunday night, the White House sent out its daily media guidance, which did not have any major broadcast outlet included for Monday’s pool duties.

Trump has attempted to ban outlets from government spaces before. He barred The Associated Press from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some events after it declined to call the Gulf of Mexico by Trump’s preferred name, the Gulf of America. The AP sued the administration, and the case is ongoing.

title: Tehran warns of ‘new weapons’ as Trump weighs meeting with Iranian president
summary: Iran warned Monday it would use “new weapons with new capabilities” if the U.S. launched a fresh assault after President Donald Trump ramped up the rhetoric against Tehran over the weekend.
story: Iran warned Monday it would use “new weapons with new capabilities” if the U.S. launched a fresh assault after President Donald Trump ramped up the rhetoric against Tehran over the weekend.

“If a new aggression takes place, we will definitely change the weapons and geography of the war,” Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Monday, according to the semiofficial Fars news agency.
Mohebbi did not provide details on what the new weapons were or which new locations could be hit.

Earlier, Trump said he would “probably” be open to meeting with his Iranian counterpart, President Masoud Pezeshkian, during the United Nations General Assembly this week, Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reported Sunday.

The possibility of a meeting offered a glimmer of hope for a resolution to the nearly seven-month war with Iran, which has resulted in Iran blocking the key Strait of Hormuz, and its Yemeni allies bombing a crucial east-west oil pipeline and threatening another crucial waterway. Resultant economic shock waves have hit the U.S. and the world economy, driving up oil and diesel prices and fueling inflation.

title: The Chiefs and Patrick Mahomes look like their old selves, but now with new help
summary: With playmakers surrounding Patrick Mahomes, and late-game moxie that helped them survive a wild overtime play, the Kansas City Chiefs improved to 2-0.
story: The Kansas City Chiefs last season lost more than Patrick Mahomes, their franchise cornerstone player, to a season-ending injury.

Well before the star quarterback injured two ligaments in his left knee last December, the Chiefs had already lost the air of invincibility they’d built while becoming the NFL’s most-feared team in close games.

That quality had earned the Chiefs three Super Bowl titles under coach Andy Reid, and a 17-game winning streak in games decided by 8 points or less. That streak was snapped in last year’s first game, and from there only got worse.

By last season’s end, their record in one-score games was 1-9, a turnaround some attributed to Mahomes’ inconsistent play before his injury, or a supporting cast of receivers and running backs had grown thin. Tight end Travis Kelce, one of the most prolific pass-catchers in the position’s history, was in the middle of one of his worst statistical seasons. On the ground, the Chiefs ranked near the league’s bottom third in yards per carry.
But two games into this new season, Kansas City is 2-0 and again looks like a team that could be feared in the AFC.

Mahomes appears uninhibited by his knee injury, and now has a number of playmakers surrounding him — led by a familiar face, and one new. And in Sunday’s 33-30 overtime win against Indianapolis, the Chiefs showed again they know how to win a close game while overcoming a wild play that might have changed the outcome.
“There was never a doubt that we were going to get that win,” Kelce said.

A walk-off 40-yard field goal as time expired by Harrison Butker gave the Chiefs their eighth consecutive overtime win in the regular season, tying an NFL record also held by San Francisco (2003-10). Mahomes, who threw for 382 yards and three touchdowns, now has 25 career game-winning drives in the fourth quarter or overtime. The Chiefs join Las Vegas, Cincinnati and Buffalo as the only remaining undefeated teams in the AFC.
“That’s what this NFL is about is just finding a way to win games,” Mahomes said on NBC’s “Sunday Night Football.”
Kansas City thought it had the game won with five minutes remaining in overtime.

Tied at 30-30, Colts quarterback Daniel Jones connected with Laquon Treadwell for a 48-yard gain down to Kansas City’s 17-yard line when Treadwell bobbled and recovered the catch while evading one tackle by L’Jarius Sneed. Trying to gain more yardage, Treadwell was then tackled by Chiefs cornerback Nohl Williams, who punched the ball out for a fumble recovered by Kansas City. Under regular-season overtime rules that have been in place since 2025 that allow each team at least one possession each, Kansas City believed it had won the game by forcing a turnover and stopping the Colts short of tying the game on its first overtime drive.

An official review, however, found that Sneed’s left hand grazed the right hip of Treadwell at the same time he secured his bobbled catch — a brush of a few fingers that was barely enough to count Treadwell as down by contact, however slight, at that moment. It negated the fumble that followed. The Colts were still alive.

A touchdown would win the game for Indianapolis, but three plays later it still wasn’t close to the end zone. On fourth and 8, 15 yards from a score, the Colts put their offense on the field and looked ready to snap if they had seen the defense they wanted. When they didn’t, the Colts kicked the field goal for a 30-30 tie. By doing so, Mahomes was left with plenty of time to mount a comeback.
“Had a play called,” Colts coach Shane Steichen said of the fourth-down decision. “Had to love the look to run it there.”

Mahomes jogged into the huddle with 3:06 remaining in overtime knowing the next score would win. He and the Chiefs made it a reality by turning to the franchise’s newest weapon, Kenneth Walker, the Most Valuable Player of last February’s Super Bowl for Seattle who became the team’s prized offseason signing as a free agent.
Walker rushed the ball three times for 18 yards, caught a 22-yard pass from Mahomes, and rushed two more yards to set up Butker’s game-winning kick.

One week after producing a career-high 191 yards from scrimmage during his Chiefs debut in Week 1, a total helped by Walker’s league-best 14 broken tackles, he finished with 117 rushing yards on 24 carries and added 61 yards receiving against the Colts. Walker has looked every bit the missing piece capable of taking pressure off of Mahomes on the ground and opening up the passing game.

“We able to, I guess, freestyle it,” Walker told NBC in a postgame interview of his connection with Mahomes. “If I’m open or if somebody open, play break down, he able to make plays, so it’s great to play with him.”

Even more encouraging for Kansas City was not just how quickly a new addition in Walker has integrated into the offense, but how much Kelce — the record-breaking tight end who helped jump-start the team’s dynasty alongside Mahomes — resembled his old self Sunday.

Kelce has debated whether to retire each of the last two offseasons after producing career-low yardage totals and just eight touchdowns combined in 2024-25. He was targeted on fewer than seven passes per game last season.

On Sunday, a faster, more agile Kelce was targeted 11 times, more than any Chiefs pass-catcher. He caught nine passes for 101 yards including a touchdown that left his pop superstar wife, Taylor Swift, pointing to her wedding ring in a suite in celebration. It was his first game with 100-plus yards and a touchdown since Week 7 of 2023. Kelce now has 128 yards after contact this season, the most in his career through a season’s first two games, per ESPN.
“We’re in a zone right now where everybody’s feeding off each other and it’s only making us better and it’s making us play harder for each other.”

The contributions from Mahomes and his co-stars, and the team’s late-game moxie, have kept the Chiefs undefeated. Still to be seen is whether those factors also can reverse a troubling trend over the course of a long season. Between 2017-22, the Chiefs ranked among the league’s 10 best in scoring every season and led the NFL in points in 2018 and 2022. In the last three years, though, they ranked 15th in both 2023 and 2024 before dropping to 21st last season.
“The parity in this league is crazy,” Chiefs coach Reid said. “You’re going to have some once-score games. You have to bear down, and our guys did that.”

title: Texas poll: James Talarico holds a narrow advantage for Senate while Greg Abbott leads for governor
summary: Democrat James Talarico holds a narrow advantage over Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race, but within the margin of error, according to a new poll, while Republican Gov.
story: Democrat James Talarico holds a narrow advantage over Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race, but within the margin of error, according to a new poll, while Republican Gov. Greg Abbott holds a wider lead over Democrat Gina Hinojosa in the contest for governor, as economic issues and immigration drive voter decision-making.

The new NBC5 Dallas/Telemundo Station Group poll shows Talarico at 46% and Paxton at 43%, within the survey’s margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. Another 8% of potential voters were still up for grabs in the race — just as tens of millions of dollars in advertising from Republican groups began to flood into the state.
Abbott took 48% to Hinojosa’s 41% in the gubernatorial race, a broader edge that’s also technically within the margin of error.

The survey effort also zeroed in on Latinos in Texas, shows how that group of voters has swung back to the left since President Donald Trump won 55% of the Hispanic vote in Texas in 2024, according to NBC News exit polling.
Both Talarico and Hinojosa led with Latinos by double digits, with Talarico up 18 points (54%-36%) and Hinojosa up 13 points (52%-39%).

But that may still fall short of the benchmark the candidates would need to pull out a victory in a state that hasn’t elected a statewide Democrat in three decades. At a UnidosUS conference in August, Hinojosa indicated a previous Democratic marker at 64% would be enough to win.

“To give you a sense of our importance in this election, in 2018, the closest a Democrat came to flipping Texas in recent history, Beto O’Rourke ran against Ted Cruz and he got 64% of the Latino vote,” Hinojosa said then. “When I get 64% of the Latino vote in 2026, I win.”
Hispanic voters hold enormous electoral power in Texas, making up about a third of the state’s electorate.

The survey included 401 Hispanic likely voters in Texas, who were interviewed live by telephone by Mason-Dixon Polling & Research, Inc. from Sept. 8-12. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 5 points. The same firm conducted the broader survey of 625 likely voters in Texas Sept. 8-10.
In both surveys, economic factors ranked the highest when it came to voter motivations, with immigration issues ranking the second-highest for Hispanic voters.
Among all voters, the top issues identified were the economy and jobs at 24%,
inflation and the cost of living at 23%, immigration and the border at 18%, and healthcare at 10%.

Among Hispanic voters, inflation and the cost of living topped their concerns, with 33% saying it had the greatest influence on their vote. The next highest concern was immigration and the border at 23%, followed by the economy and jobs at 19%, and healthcare at 9%. Crime and public safety, education and housing all ranked in the single digits.

Overall, Texas voters lined up strongly in favor of restrictions on gender transition-related medical treatments for minors, with 63% supporting and 29% opposing restrictions. On a related question, 61% of respondents believed students should only use the bathroom for the sex they were assigned at birth and 8% saying students should be allowed to use the bathroom for the gender with which they identify. Most of the remainder said schools should provide gender-neutral bathrooms.

Notably, however, social issues such as abortion and trans rights ranked low on the list of issues that voters said would influence their candidate choices. Overall, abortion and trans rights ranked at 6% importance among all groups and at 4% among Hispanic voters.
That low mark is significant, as Republican super PACs have already spent millions of dollars on TV and digital ads, particularly targeting Talarico, with messaging squarely focused on trans issues.

Voters statewide were more or less split on whether Texas should cooperate with ICE on vehicle pursuits and traffic stops. While Hispanic voters were about evenly split on the question — 45% saying Texas should cooperate, 48% saying it shouldn’t ––  white voters were far more favorable toward cooperation: 62% in support of cooperation, 32% against it.
It was the reverse for Black voters. Of those surveyed, 66% of Black voters say the state should not cooperate with ICE on the stops and 24% said it should.
Immigration questions broke sharply along ideological lines.

In the survey of all Texas voters, 93% of Republicans said local police officers should be allowed to question individuals about their immigration status during lawful encounters, while 11% of Democrats and 50% of independents supported the policy.

The surveys explored other areas, including a question on a voucher program that’s been controversial in the state. Sixty-three percent of those queried said they opposed allowing state tax dollars to be used to pay for private school tuition, with 30% supporting it and another 7% undecided statewide.

title: Elon Musk is flying under the radar in the Texas Senate race. Republicans like it that way.
summary: The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 state Supreme Court race in Wisconsin.
story: The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 state Supreme Court race in Wisconsin. He donned an oversized cheese hat, offered $1 million checks to voters, and he and affiliated groups poured at least $20 million into the contest.
In the end, the conservative candidate lost by 10 points in what was widely viewed as a rebuke of Musk and the Trump administration.

Now, the richest person in the world is back boosting Republican candidates in critical midterm elections, including a bruising Senate race in Texas where Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democrat James Talarico, who had initially far outraised him and remains close in polling.
But that financial tide is quickly turning — with Musk’s help.

Unlike in Wisconsin, Musk has so far stayed out of the spotlight in Texas, even though he lives in the state, has based his companies Tesla and SpaceX there, and employs about 20,000 people. He hasn’t announced plans for any in-person events, or teased — as he did in Wisconsin — that he’d be handing out $1 million checks to voters.

Privately, Republicans say they want Musk to keep his distance. In interviews, more than half a dozen Republican strategists involved in the Texas Senate race say they hope Musk follows his 2024 model of electoral involvement, which led to a Republican sweep of the White House and Congress. Then, Musk spent more than $250 million on Donald Trump and his party.

Republicans believe Democrats will attempt to turn Musk into a boogeyman if he takes on a higher-profile role in Texas or other battlegrounds. One Republican consultant involved in the Texas Senate race said that was the perception in Wisconsin.

“He came in super late, and it was very public,” said the consultant, who, like others interviewed for this article, were granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Elon spending money became the story, which I think maybe was a mistake.”
A different Republican strategist involved in Texas campaigns said those around Musk learned from the experience.
“Did Elon bring some things to the Wisconsin race that hampered things? Probably,” the person added. “But I think they will adjust for that.”
Add to Google
Add to Google
Democrats, however, say they welcome Musk more publicly entering the fray in Texas.

“Elon, bring it. You’ve failed in Wisconsin. You’ll fail in Texas,” said Nathan Johnson, a Democrat running to replace Paxton as attorney general. “I’m not afraid of Elon bringing his political money here. All these policies favor him or people like him.”

An in-your-face Musk campaign would play into Talarico’s narrative that the real American divide isn’t left versus right but “top versus bottom,” with elites and billionaires exerting control over the working class, they say.

“James is running largely on costs and corruption,” Luke Warford, a Texas-based Democratic strategist and chair of the Travis County Democratic Party, said of Talarico. “The idea of the richest man in the world coming in late to try to buy the election and save Ken Paxton really plays into James Talarico’s argument.”

The Texas Senate race has all the makings of a contest that would attract Musk. The conservative narrative building against Talarico amplifies his past remarks in support of transgender people, including his comment that “God is nonbinary.” Talarico told Fox News he was being “provocative” and was trying to convey that one cannot use “human categories to define God.”

Musk has spoken publicly about his own transgender daughter, Vivian Jenna Wilson, saying she was “not a girl” and was figuratively “dead.” He also alleged that he had been “tricked” into authorizing trans-related medical treatment for her when she was 16. Wilson previously told NBC News that Musk was an absent father who was cruel to her as a child for being queer and feminine.

At this point, Musk’s America PAC has not said how much it will invest in Texas, but a person with knowledge of the group’s thinking indicated that as of now, the Paxton-Talarico contest was not slotted to receive more focus than other Senate or congressional races the group is investing in across the country, saying “every state and district where we are spending is a priority.”
To date, America PAC has spent nearly $5.2 million on digital ads, mail, live calls and pamphleting in Texas, but that number is expected to significantly climb.

In all, the super PAC has spent $14.7 million on congressional races, including seven Senate races and nearly three dozen House races. The group has spent the most money on the Texas Senate race, followed by nearly $3 million on Senate races in Ohio and Michigan.

National Republican groups long knew they would have to provide air cover for Paxton because of an initial fundraising disadvantage to Talarico, who had $21 million in cash on hand compared to Paxton’s $1.7 million at the end of June, according to campaign finance reports. Today, a flood of Republican money is pouring in from several sources and the balance has suddenly tipped in Paxton’s favor.

“America PAC is working in full coordination with the entire GOP apparatus and is investing in the states and districts that will decide control of the House and Senate,” America PAC spokesman Andrew Romeo said in a statement. “Our only priority is ensuring Republicans keep full control of Washington and stopping the lunatic left from bringing us back to the days of open borders, rampant crime, and woke policies.”

Paxton’s status as a scandal-plagued candidate who has been impeached and indicted — coupled with the fact he’s coming off a contentious primary against Sen. John Cornyn and much of the Republican Party establishment, aside from Trump — makes him among the most vulnerable front-line Senate Republican candidates in a state where Democrats have not won a statewide post in three decades.

After Trump’s late endorsement helped propel Paxton over Cornyn, groups like the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, were left scrambling. The election cycle budgets were, in part, built on the idea that Cornyn would not need nearly as much national fundraising help.

“Cornyn had his own fundraising machine, he could raise a lot of money on his own, so it was going to make things easier to cover other important close races,” said a Republican consultant familiar with the thought process. “I know they [Elon] are focused more on the ground game stuff. MAGA Inc. is on digital and mail. This pretty much turned out the way we thought it would. It’s an expensive endeavor and a team and multigroup effort.”
The pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC has pumped at least $15 million into TV ads that have included hitting Talarico on previous votes involving China.
So far, MAGA Inc. has spent $10 million in the state to help boost Paxton, its second-biggest single-state investment.

The group did not return a request for comment, but in an interview with NBC News last week, MAGA Inc. chief James Blair said the group had booked $10 million worth of TV ad time in Texas. Blair noted the previous disparity in spending, with Talarico and related groups pummeling Paxton on TV.

“The fact is Ken Paxton had $100 million spent against him in the primary,” Blair said. “Talarico had $0 spent against him in the primary, and that has an impact on candidate images that takes time to rectify. But the resources … have begun to be deployed now in earnest [and] will take care of that problem.”
A veteran GOP official directly involved in the race contended that the shift toward spending in Texas did not take away from other battlegrounds.

“This spending will not take away from other investments,” the official said. “This came from a collection of Texas folks very committed to making sure that seat remains Republican. They see the polling, and that James Talarico is so extreme. No one wants to see Texas turn blue.”

When asked about the onslaught of money headed toward Talarico, spokesman JT Ennis said, “Billionaire-backed dark money groups are lying about James because they’re scared of the people-powered movement we’re building to fix this broken, corrupt political system.”

title: Cindy Crawford’s son, model Presley Gerber, dies at 27
summary: Presley Gerber, the son of supermodel Cindy Crawford, died Sunday, a family representative said in a statement.
story: Presley Gerber, the son of supermodel Cindy Crawford, died Sunday, a family representative said in a statement.
He was 27.
Gerber died at a “rehab facility,” according to online records of the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner. No cause of death or further detail was given.
“The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time,” a statement on behalf of his family said.
Supermodel Crawford married businessman Rande Gerber in 1998, and they have two children.
Gerber and his younger sister, Kaia, both became professional models, featuring in campaigns for Dolce & Gabbana and Calvin Klein, among others.
At 18, Gerber featured alongside his mother in a 2018 ad to re-create her iconic 1992 Super Bowl commercial for Pepsi.
He and his sister have spoken about their mother giving them professional space.
“She has never lived vicariously through us,” Kaia Gerber said in a family interview with “TODAY” last year.
“You are so not a stage mom,” she added, of her mother.

Gerber had posted online frequently about his struggles with depression and addiction. He instigated a program called “Mental Health Mondays” on his Instagram account, where he spoke openly about his struggles. He said in doing so he had hoped to “spark real conversations about the stuff most people hide.”
In November, he wrote that he “had to step back and take care of my own mental health for a bit.”
In an interview with Vogue magazine last month, his sister spoke about his struggles.

“My parents for most of our lives were very, very private and didn’t share anything — and now we have this absolute teacher, my brother, who says, ‘I’m gonna be very human for everyone,’” she said. “There’s only so much you can hide from the world. And trying to put a lid on something just makes the person feel like you’re ashamed of them.”

In July, for her son’s 27th birthday, Crawford posted two images online featuring Gerber as a child and as a young teenager, writing: “I’m so proud of the man you’ve become, but I’ll always see you as my little boy! Love you.”

If you or someone you know is struggling or in emotional distress, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org 24/7 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For additional resources, visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources.

title: U.S. proposes AI alert system with China ahead of Trump-Xi summit
summary: The United States has proposed a new AI safety notification mechanism for President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to consider at their summit in Washington this week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday.
story: HONG KONG — The United States has proposed a new AI safety notification mechanism for President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to consider at their summit in Washington this week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday, amid global concern over whether the world’s two leading AI powers can work together to contain the technology’s potential dangers.

Speaking to reporters after daylong talks in New York with Chinese officials, Bessent said the two sides had discussed setting up a new U.S.-China AI dialogue that would include a mechanism for alerting each other to AI-related incidents that could affect national security.

“We think that just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important,” he said, adding that the two sides had agreed to meet again on the AI issue.
'Godfather of AI': Congress has about a year to get ahead of AI

AI is expected to be high on the agenda when Trump and Xi meet Thursday, especially after warnings from AI leaders in the U.S. that the technology could pose an existential threat within a few years. Trump has dismissed such concerns as a “hoax” while agreeing with AI executives such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei that the U.S. must not allow China to pull ahead in the global AI race.

Experts caution that the Trump-Xi summit is unlikely to produce any major agreement on AI, citing the high level of distrust between the two countries. China has interpreted calls to slow down AI development as targeted at its own progress.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters that AI talks would not affect U.S. export controls on advanced chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment that have hindered Chinese AI companies.

Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng and China’s chief trade negotiator, Li Chenggang, did not comment to reporters as they left the talks at JPMorganChase headquarters. A Chinese readout of the talks published by Xinhua, China’s state-run news agency, did not mention the U.S. proposal and said only that the two sides had discussed AI.

Xinhua said the two sides also had “frank, in-depth and constructive exchanges on important economic and trade issues of common concern, including implementing the consensus reached in previous trade consultations and promoting bilateral trade and investment.”
A major question ahead of this week’s summit is whether Trump and Xi will agree to extend a fragile trade truce that is set to expire Nov. 10.

Bessent and Greer said the two sides had agreed to operationalize a new “Board of Trade” that was announced during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May, and were exploring the potential for lower tariffs on “non-sensitive” products.

On the Chinese side, Greer said, those could include consumer goods and low-tech items, while U.S. exports of energy, agricultural goods and medical devices are also being considered. He did not say whether that meant tariffs on those items would be lowered now or that they would only be exempted from fresh duties in the future.

“There is a world where you have a relatively small subset of American and Chinese goods that can be traded in a balanced way that are non-sensitive,” he said. “Then in the future, as trade actions come up, we can consider them as a class unto themselves.”
Jennifer Jett reported from Hong Kong, and Steve Kopack and Allie Canal reported from New York.

title: Le Creuset’s deep Dutch oven is almost 40% off right now
summary: Le Creuset’s popular Dutch oven is almost 40% off including a recently launched shade. Shop the deal if you want a durable pot that will last years in the kitchen.
story: If you know anyone who owns anything from Le Creuset, then you know that they likely guard it with their life. That’s because Le Creuset Dutch ovens and skillets aren’t just for show — they’re an investment. And right now, Le Creuset’s Signature Dutch Oven is   nearly 40 percent off at Williams Sonoma.
